traveler: Saint Cyriacus of Rome (Kyriakos, Ciriaco, Cyriakus, Cyriaque), deacon and martyr
title: The Deacon in the Baths: Two Exorcisms, a Milestone on the Via Ostiensis, and the Arm That Goes to Alsace
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Nobleman Who Gives It Away

stops.name: Rome, the patrician who gives it away
stops.date_confidence: invented placeholder to force a starting pin. No source consulted gives a birth year, a quarter of Rome, a family, or parents. The coordinate is the city centroid, not a located house
stops.campa: A son is born into a patrician house in Rome, and no source names the quarter, the year, or the family. The tradition that reaches English readers says only this: he is a Roman nobleman who converts to Christianity as an adult, sells what he owns, and gives the money to the poor. Everything else about the beginning is silence. The name he carries, Kyriakos, is Greek for belonging to the lord. A freedman is called that, and so is a church building. The ambiguity outlives him by seventeen centuries.
suggested_refs: The Greek kyriakos, 'belonging to the lord', as both a personal name and a term for a church

stops.name: Alexandria, the other origin
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated. The German strand gives no year for the Alexandrian training; 290 positions it before the Roman ministry and nothing more
stops.campa: A second strand of the legend, carried in German, makes him no Roman patrician at all but a physician and exorcist trained at Alexandria, arriving in Rome with a craft already in his hands. Catherine of Alexandria walks this same city in the atlas, a few years later and under a different emperor. No source reconciles the two origins. One tradition gives him wealth to renounce, the other gives him a technique to practise, and the exorcisms he is later famous for fit the second story better than the first.
suggested_refs: The two incompatible origin traditions, Roman patrician and Alexandrian physician, unreconciled in any source

stops.name: Rome, the diaconate under a contested pope
stops.date_confidence: contested three ways. de.wikipedia gives the ordination as 'um 300' under Marcellinus; it.wikipedia names Marcellus I, pope only from 308, which is after the usual year of death; en.wikipedia never calls him a deacon at all. The pool's earlier date of 296 appears in no source and was struck
stops.campa: He is ordained deacon of the Roman church, and the sources cannot agree who ordains him. The German tradition puts it around 300 under Marcellinus. The Italian names Marcellus the First, who is pope only from 308, five years after the year usually given for the death. English Wikipedia never calls him a deacon at all. A deacon in Rome administers the alms and buries the poor, which is the work the legend will describe him doing, whoever handed him the office.
suggested_refs: The three-way disagreement over the ordaining pope: Marcellinus, Marcellus I, or no diaconate

stops.name: Baths of Diocletian, the water carried into the cutting
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources. The Baths were under construction 298 to 306; the year 298 that circulated in the research pool appears in no source and was removed as a plausible-looking invention
stops.campa: The emperor is raising the largest baths in the city, and Christians condemned to the works haul stone in the cutting. Cyriacus spends the rest of his life among them. The group journey of the Fourteen Holy Helpers puts it plainly: the persecution that kills him is paid for, in part, by their stone. No source says he baptizes them, and no source says they are conscripts rather than convicts. The sources say he ministers to the slaves who work in the Baths of Diocletian. They say nothing more than that.
sources: catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, stop 'Via Salaria, the deacon buried by the road'
suggested_refs: The Baths of Diocletian, under construction 298 to 306, and the condemned labour on them

stops.name: Rome, Thrason's bread reaches the cells
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source. The Orthodox synaxarion narrative gives no year; 302 places the episode before the edicts of 303 and is a positioning placeholder
stops.campa: A rich Christian named Thrason funds a relief operation for the prisoners, and four men carry it in: Sisinius the deacon, Cyriacus, Smaragdus, Largus. The three names that will be executed beside him are already in the room. The Orthodox synaxarion keeps this detail where the Latin tradition loses it, and it is the only glimpse of the deacon at ordinary work, hands full of bread and cloth, before the machinery takes him. The account is a modern English rendering of a Greek text, not the ancient passio.
stops.quote: A certain rich Christian, Thrason, sent food and clothing to the prisoners through the Christians Sisinius, Cyriacus, Smaragdus and Largus.
stops.quote_source: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him', commemorated 7 June
sources: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him'
suggested_refs: The Greek synaxarion account of Sisinius and his companions, in the OCA's English rendering

stops.name: Rome, the tripods melt
stops.date_confidence: undated legendary episode, positioned inside the pre-edict imprisonment. No source assigns it a year
stops.campa: Saturninus, one of the company, prays aloud in front of the idols and the bronze goes soft. The synaxarion sets the prayer and its answer in consecutive sentences with nothing between them, which is how this kind of account works: the request and the melting are one event. Cyriacus is in the same narrative and the same prison, though the miracle is not credited to him. The group is being written as a group, and the powers move among them without much regard for which name holds them.
stops.quote: At that very moment the tripods, on which incense burned before the idols, melted.
stops.quote_source: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him', commemorated 7 June
sources: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him'
suggested_refs: Saturninus's prayer and the melted tripods, in the same synaxarion narrative that carries Cyriacus

stops.name: Rome, the jailer sees the light
stops.date_confidence: undated legendary episode. The conversion of Apronian is placed here inside the same imprisonment, with no year given by any source
stops.campa: Apronian, the officer set to guard them, looks at Sisinius in the cell and converts on the spot. He is baptized and joins the list of the condemned. This is the pattern the whole dossier runs on: the possessed are cleaned, the guards change sides, the emperor's own household goes over, and the executions happen anyway. The reputation of Cyriacus as a healer and a caster-out of devils is built inside this prison, and the emperor will hear of it from his own staff.
stops.quote: seeing his face shine with a heavenly light, he believed in Christ and was baptized
stops.quote_source: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him', on the prison officer Apronian
sources: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him'
suggested_refs: The conversion of the guard Apronian, one of the recurring conversion-miracles of the group's passio

segments.name: The Year the Edicts Go Up

stops.name: Nicomedia, the church pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the edict itself. The causal link between this edict and the death of Cyriacus at Rome the same year is an inference drawn by the atlas from the shared year and the shared administration, stated by no source. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from constantino_el_grande.journey.json
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of February the first edict of the Great Persecution goes up at Nicomedia: churches razed, scriptures surrendered, Christians stripped of rank and of standing at law. Constantine is thirty and at court that week, and the atlas records that he says nothing anyone writes down. The order travels west along the imperial post to Rome, where a deacon is already in custody. The edict is documented. Everything that happens to Cyriacus under it is not.
sources: constantino_el_grande.journey.json, stop 'Nicomedia, the church pulled down'
suggested_refs: The first edict of the Great Persecution, posted at Nicomedia 23 February 303

stops.name: Baalbek, the tower in the same persecution
stops.date_confidence: the 303 edict backdrop is attested in saint_barbara.journey.json; the tie to Cyriacus's own death in that year is inferred by juxtaposition and by later company membership, not stated in either file. The month is a sequencing placeholder only. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from saint_barbara.journey.json
stops.campa: In Heliopolis a merchant's daughter is shut in a tower, and the edicts of 303 are nailed up in the provincial forum outside it. Barbara will be killed by her own father. Cyriacus will be killed by the state. The atlas puts them in the same year and the same list, and the list is what survives them both. Only the persecution is attested here. The link between the two deaths is drawn by the calendar and by a Franconian devotion eleven centuries later, not by anything either dossier says about the other.
sources: saint_barbara.journey.json, stop 'Baalbek, the beauty that draws suitors'
suggested_refs: The edicts of 303 posted in the provincial fora, backdrop to Barbara's confinement at Heliopolis

stops.name: Rome, the palace and the possessed boy
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated in the Vitus sources, placed inside the traditional martyrdom year by san_vito.journey.json, which dates it 0303-01-01; the month here is a sequencing placeholder. The overlap with Cyriacus is drawn by juxtaposition; neither legend mentions the other. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from san_vito.journey.json
stops.campa: Vitus is brought to Rome the same year, exorcises a spirit out of the emperor's household, refuses to sacrifice, and survives a cauldron and the lions before the gibbet. Cyriacus is in the same city, doing the same work on the same household, in the same year. The two legends never mention each other. They are two tellings of one story that Roman hagiography kept reusing: the imperial child possessed, the Christian prisoner who can do what the priests cannot, the gratitude that does not save him.
sources: san_vito.journey.json, stop 'Rome, the palace, the possessed boy'
suggested_refs: The recurring Roman exorcism-at-the-palace motif, shared by the legends of Vitus and Cyriacus

stops.name: Byzantium, the centurion beheaded in the same year
stops.date_confidence: conventional for Acacius, whose year is given as 303 or c. 304 and whose feast sits on 8 May, 7 May, or 17 April depending on the calendar. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from saint_acacius.journey.json
stops.campa: Acacius, a Cappadocian serving as centurion in the garrison, refuses to sacrifice, is scourged, and is beheaded in a town that does not yet carry Constantine's name. Blaise of Sebaste, killed thirteen years later, will be put in the same list by the same devotion. Acacius and Cyriacus will stand first and sixth in that list eleven hundred years on, and neither man knows the other exists. The company of fourteen is assembled backwards, from the graves.
sources: saint_blaise.journey.json, stop 'Byzantium, the persecution already running'
suggested_refs: The 303 cohort of the Fourteen: Acacius at Byzantium, Vitus at Rome, Barbara at Heliopolis

stops.name: Rome, the emperor sends for the prisoner
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated. Wikipedia flags the whole strand for 'chronological impossibilities' without enumerating them; the month here is a positioning placeholder inside the edict year
stops.campa: Artemia, called Artemisia in some tellings, is possessed, and she is the daughter of Diocletian. The emperor who has just signed the edict sends to the cells for a Christian. Cyriacus casts the demon out and the girl converts. Wikipedia flags the whole strand for chronological impossibilities and does not enumerate them. The scene is the centre of everything remembered about him, and it is the part of the dossier with the least support of any kind.
stops.quote: Having learned that the prisoner Cyriacus could heal infirmities and cast out devils, the emperor summoned him to the sick girl.
stops.quote_source: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him', commemorated 7 June
sources: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him'
suggested_refs: The exorcism of Artemia, daughter of Diocletian, the central episode of the legend

stops.name: Rome, Serena and the house on the hill
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated. The house-gift detail belongs to de.wikipedia, not to the Golden Legend as the research pool first recorded, and de.wikipedia does not identify the house with the site of the later titular church
stops.campa: Artemia's mother Serena, the emperor's wife, converts with her daughter. The German tradition adds that Diocletian in gratitude gives Cyriacus a house, and that he sets up a chapel inside it. The tradition does not say the house stands where the titular church of Saint Cyriacus will later stand, though every retelling wants it to. English Wikipedia offers a flatter etymology: Roman tituli were named for their patrons, and Kyriakos in Greek signifies simply patron. The church may hold no martyr at all.
suggested_refs: The competing accounts of the titulus name: an emperor's gift, or the Greek word for patron

stops.name: Ctesiphon, the king's daughter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction pin. No source names the Persian city; Ctesiphon stands here only as the Sasanian capital of the period. The month is a positioning placeholder inside the legendary sequence
stops.campa: A Persian king's daughter named Jobia is possessed, and the deacon is sent east across the frontier to treat her. No source names the city; Ctesiphon stands here because it is the Sasanian capital of the period. He travels as a prisoner released on a commission, across a border two empires have been fighting over for seventy years, at the invitation of a court that never appears again in his story. He cures her, and the king's household is baptized, and then the account turns around and comes home.
suggested_refs: The Persian episode of the passio, unlocated by any source

stops.name: Ctesiphon, the king who was already dead
stops.date_confidence: documented impossibility rather than uncertainty. en.wikipedia names Shapur I, reigned 241 to 272, and states the episode 'is impossible, because Shapur died thirty years before the reputed exorcism and because he had only one daughter named Adur-Anahid'. Narseh (293 to 303) and Hormizd II (303 to 309) are proposed as substitutes
stops.campa: The king the legend names is Shapur the First, who died in 272, thirty years before the exorcism, and who had one daughter named Adur-Anahid and no Jobia. This is not a date that cannot be checked. It is a date that has been checked and fails. Later commentators offer Narseh, who reigns until 303, or Hormizd the Second, who reigns from 303, and both are substitutions made to keep the story upright. The Persian journey is the one episode the sources themselves refuse to defend.
suggested_refs: Shapur I, Narseh and Hormizd II, three kings proposed for one impossible exorcism

stops.name: Rome, the return
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried, not resolved. The hagiographic tradition dates the return from Persia to 304 while dating the execution to 303, which is impossible in sequence. The stop is placed in July 303 to keep the journey in travel order; the 304 return date is the source's, and it is wrong or the death date is
stops.campa: He comes back to Rome from Persia, into a city where the edicts have been running for months. The chronology has already broken: the tradition puts the return in 304 and the execution in 303, and no teller has ever noticed. He returns to a house given him by the emperor whose daughter he cured, in a persecution ordered by that same emperor, and the legend does not treat this as a difficulty either. Nothing in the account explains what he expects to find waiting.
suggested_refs: The impossible sequence: a return dated 304 preceding an execution dated 303

stops.name: Rome, taken under Maximian
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated; the place of arrest is unrecorded. en.wikipedia names Maximian as the arresting authority, the OCA account names Galerius, and popular summaries name Diocletian. Three emperors for one arrest
stops.campa: The arrest is made under Maximian, the western augustus, not under Diocletian, who is in the East. The place is not recorded. The gratitude of the palace, if the palace was ever grateful, does not reach as far as the co-emperor's officers, and the man who cured the imperial daughter goes back into the cells he had been carrying bread into. The Orthodox account puts Galerius in this role instead. Three emperors are named for one arrest across three traditions, and no two agree.
sources: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him'
suggested_refs: The disagreement over the persecuting emperor: Maximian, Galerius, or Diocletian

stops.name: Rome, dragged behind the chariot
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated; placed a week before the traditional feast to keep the sequence. The OCA narrative attributes the order to Galerius
stops.campa: The synaxarion has the emperor put him behind the chariot and drive him through Rome, stripped and chained, for the crowds to see. The punishment is a display rather than an execution, and it is aimed at the reputation the prison built: the man who could cast out devils is shown unable to keep his own clothes. The Orthodox account then has him die under torture. The Latin account has him beheaded. The two churches that keep him do not keep the same death.
stops.quote: He gave orders to drag Cyriacus behind his chariot stripped, bloodied, and in chains, to be shamed and ridiculed by the crowds.
stops.quote_source: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him', commemorated 7 June
sources: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 'Hieromartyr Sisinius the Deacon of Rome and Those with Him'
suggested_refs: The internal inconsistency of the OCA account, which has Cyriacus die under torture and his companions beheaded

stops.name: Rome, the boiling oil
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated, and present in only one language tradition. de.wikipedia carries the boiling oil; the English and Italian accounts of the same trial do not
stops.campa: Before sentence the German tradition has him tortured with boiling oil poured over him. The detail appears in de.wikipedia and in the iconography, and it appears in neither the English nor the Italian account of the same trial. Torture-catalogues are the least stable part of any passio, added and dropped by copyists according to what a local congregation wanted to hear. What holds across every version is the sequence itself: prison, refusal, pain, road, blade.
suggested_refs: The boiling-oil torture, carried by the German tradition alone

stops.name: Via Salaria, the deacon beheaded
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and the tag was corrected downward during verification. en.wikipedia introduces the entire episode with 'However, legend has it that...' and limits the certain record to the names, the fact of martyrdom, and the burial. The year is 303 in English sources, 16 March 306 in it.wikipedia, and 'um 309' in de.wikipedia's metadata against 'um 303' in its own lead. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json; Porta Salaria itself stood at 41.9089, 12.4953, and no source gives the milestone
stops.campa: He is beheaded on the Via Salaria with Largus and Smaragdus and about twenty others, among them Crescentianus and the women Memmia and Juliana. The Roman Martyrology carries only those three companion names; the longer roster of twenty comes from Alban Butler. English Wikipedia opens the whole episode with the words however, legend has it, and limits the certain record to the names, the fact of the martyrdom, and the burial. The road is tradition. The grave is documented.
sources: catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, stop 'Via Salaria, the deacon buried by the road'
suggested_refs: The Roman Martyrology's three named companions against Alban Butler's roster of twenty

stops.name: The seventh milestone of the Via Ostiensis, the bodies moved
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the burial site and the day, uncertain as to the year. The coordinate is about 11.3 km southwest of Porta San Paolo, roughly the 7.6th Roman mile, nearer Vitinia and Malafede than Acilia. The afterlife lens of this research pinned the same site at 41.8218, 12.4308, roughly the fifth mile; the two cannot both be right and the discrepancy is recorded rather than reconciled
stops.campa: The Salaria runs northeast out of Rome and the Ostiensis runs southwest to the sea, and the bodies are on the wrong road. The Italian tradition supplies the missing move: Pope Marcellus the First has them carried from the Via Salaria to the seventh milestone of the Via Ostiensis. That transfer is the origin of the eighth of August, which is a burial date and not a death date. Everything the churches keep about this man hangs on a milestone in the fields south of the city.
stops.quote: Of the Saint Cyriacus who, together with Saints Largus and Smaragdus and others... is venerated on 8 August, all that is known with certainty, apart from their names and the fact of their martyrdom, is that they were buried at the seventh milestone of the Via Ostiensis on that date.
stops.quote_source: en.wikipedia, 'Cyriacus', summarizing Calendarium Romanum (1969), p. 133. A secondary paraphrase, not a primary document
suggested_refs: The translation from the Via Salaria to the Via Ostiensis, attributed to Pope Marcellus I

stops.name: Rome, the title in the Baths
stops.date_confidence: attested. Marcianus is cardinal priest of the titulus in 494 under Gelasius I, per en.wikipedia. Whether the church takes its name from the martyr or the martyr's legend takes its setting from the church is not settled by any source
stops.campa: A titulus called Sanctus Ciriacus in Thermis Diocletiani is on record by 494, when Marcianus is its cardinal priest under Gelasius the First. It stands in the ruin of the baths where the legend has him carrying water, which is either the neatest confirmation in the whole dossier or the source of the legend itself. Nothing in the record says which way the borrowing runs. A church needs a patron and a patron needs a story, and by 494 both are in place.
suggested_refs: The titulus Sanctus Ciriacus in Thermis Diocletiani, attested 494

stops.name: Santa Maria in Via Lata, the relics claimed
stops.date_confidence: placeholder for 'early medieval'. en.wikipedia phrases the translation as an unverified claim, 'It is claimed his relics were moved to Santa Maria in Via Lata in Rome', and gives no year; the 800 that circulated in the research pool appears in no source. The tag was corrected from attested to tradition
stops.campa: The relics are said to be moved to Santa Maria in Via Lata on the Corso. English Wikipedia phrases it as a claim and gives no date; the year here is a placeholder for early medieval. The church's own article files its Cyriacus dedication under Quiriacus of Ostia, who died about 235 and is feasted on the twenty-third of August. Either the relics lie here under the wrong label, or another saint's shrine has been absorbed into this dossier, and no source consulted decides between the two.
suggested_refs: The Quiriacus of Ostia dedication at Santa Maria in Via Lata, against the claim of the deacon's relics

stops.name: Rome, suppressed and restored and suppressed
stops.date_confidence: attested. Suppressed 1477 by Sixtus IV in favour of Saints Ciro e Giulitta, restored 1493 by Alexander VI under the name S. Ciriaco, suppressed definitively 1587 by Sixtus V. The research pool's claim that a station church survives in Rome is false and was struck
stops.campa: Sixtus the Fourth suppresses the title in 1477 in favour of Saints Ciro e Giulitta. Alexander the Sixth restores it under the name San Ciriaco in 1493. Sixtus the Fifth suppresses it definitively in 1587 and gives the title of Quirico e Giulitta to Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici. Three popes in a hundred and ten years cannot decide whether the name belongs on the map of Rome. No church of that title survives, and the deacon loses the one address in the city that was ever his.
suggested_refs: The suppression of 1587 under Sixtus V, after which no church of the title survives in Rome

stops.name: Santa Maria in Via Lata, Odazzi paints him beside Catherine
stops.date_confidence: undated by the source, which describes the painting without giving a year. Odazzi worked c. 1680 to 1731 and the date is a positioning placeholder inside that span
stops.campa: In the chapel to the left of the apse, Giovanni Odazzi paints a Madonna and child with Saints Cyriac and Catherine. The deacon stands in a Roman church beside Catherine of Alexandria, who travels the atlas in her own right and who shares his company of fourteen. The painting is the one unambiguous survival of his cult at this address. A convent called Santa Ciriaco that some accounts place nearby is absent from the church's own record and is left out here for want of a second source.
stops.quote: In the chapel to the left of the apse, is a Madonna with child and Saints Cyriac and Catherine by Giovanni Odazzi
suggested_refs: Giovanni Odazzi's Madonna with Saints Cyriac and Catherine, Santa Maria in Via Lata

stops.name: Neuhausen by Worms, Bishop Samuel fetches them
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Lorsch monastery tradition and corroborated by de.wikipedia's article on the Cyriakusstift, which credits Bishop Samuel of Worms with fetching the relics from Rome in 847. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 49.6519, 8.3742 to the article's own 49.6444, 8.3524, a shift of about 1.8 km
stops.campa: Bishop Samuel of Worms brings relics of Cyriacus up from Rome in 847, and a collegiate church goes up for them at Neuhausen outside the walls. The Lorsch monastery keeps the record. This is the first time the bones cross the Alps, and the Rhineland cult that will eventually make him one of the Fourteen begins here, three hundred years before anyone in Franconia counts to fourteen. The Roman deacon becomes a German saint by carriage, in the reign of Louis the German.
suggested_refs: The Lorsch monastery record of the 847 translation to Neuhausen

stops.name: Gernrode, Gero comes back from Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested for 963. The convent is founded in 959 and dedicated to Mary and Peter; Gero returns from Rome with the relic and the church is rededicated to Cyriacus in 963. The research pool's 'around 950' for the relic was struck as impossible, since it would precede the foundation it re-dedicates. Coordinate contradiction inside the pool, flagged: the geography lens gives 51.7228, 11.1467 and the afterlife lens 51.7233, 11.1414
stops.campa: Margrave Gero founds a convent at Gernrode in 959 and dedicates its church to Mary and Peter. In 963 he comes back from Rome with a relic of Cyriacus, and the dedication changes to the new saint. The building is one of the earliest hall-gallery basilicas north of the Alps and it is standing now, an Evangelical parish church on the Strasse der Romanik, monument-protected since 1960. A relic carried over the mountains outranks the apostle it displaces, and the stone keeps the newer name.
suggested_refs: The Stiftskirche St. Cyriakus at Gernrode, rededicated 963 on the arrival of the relic

stops.name: Altorf, the abbey founded in the Nordgau
stops.date_confidence: attested. Founded 974 by Hugues IV of Nordgau and his wife Helwilde, per fr.wikipedia, under a dedication that is not yet Cyriacus. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 48.5325, 7.6339, about 7.4 km too far east and in open country. The interlock lens reported an atlas pin of 48.5734, 7.4353, which corresponds to no stop in catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, where Altorf appears only inside a suggested_refs string
stops.campa: Hugues the Fourth of Nordgau and his wife Helwilde found a Benedictine abbey at Altorf in the Bas-Rhin in 974, under a dedication that is not yet his. The relic that will rename the house has not arrived. Alsace at this date has no particular reason to know the name of a Roman deacon, and the abbey is a family foundation of a comital line, endowed for the ordinary reasons. Cyriacus will arrive here the way he arrived at Gernrode, in a reliquary, behind a pope.
suggested_refs: The 974 foundation charter of Altorf, before the Cyriacus dedication

stops.name: Altorf, Leo IX gives the arm
stops.date_confidence: attested as mid-eleventh century, not to a single year; Leo IX is pope 1049 to 1054. The research pool treated fr.wikipedia's Leo IX and de.wikipedia's Leo X as a 460-year contradiction; they are two separate gifts, and that false contradiction is retired here
stops.campa: Pope Leo the Ninth, an Alsatian himself, consecrates the abbey altar in the middle of the eleventh century and gives the house relics, among them the arm of Saint Cyriacus. He becomes principal patron and the abbey takes his name. A reliquary bust is made for the arm, wooden at the core in the twelfth century, plated with metal in the first half of the thirteenth, restored in 1883. Four and a half centuries after Leo the Ninth, Leo the Tenth sends further portions into Alsace, and the two gifts are not one gift.
stops.quote: offrit des reliques dont le bras de saint Cyriaque
stops.quote_source: fr.wikipedia, 'Abbaye d'Altorf', on Pope Leo IX's consecration of the altar
suggested_refs: The Altorf reliquary bust: twelfth-century wooden core, thirteenth-century plating, restored 1883 to 1884

stops.name: Neuhausen, the lazaretto burns
stops.date_confidence: attested as the 1790s, during the War of the First Coalition; de.wikipedia gives no exact year and 1795 is a positioning placeholder inside that war
stops.campa: The Cyriakusstift at Neuhausen is put to use as a lazaretto and then burned by French Revolutionary troops during the War of the First Coalition. Nine hundred and fifty years after Bishop Samuel carried the bones up from Rome, the house that held them is ash. Nothing in the record says what became of the relics. Rome suppressed his title in 1587 and the Republic burned his church in the 1790s, and the two great Cyriacus addresses are lost inside two centuries of each other.

stops.name: Kitzingen, the battle fought on his day
